BM Energy (BD) Limited · Plant 1201 · SAP maintenance record, 9 February 2022 – 6 November 2026 (last order 14 October 2026)

552 maintenance orders: where the money goes, and which vehicle will break down next

A full analysis of 552 SAP PM maintenance orders: cost, preventive work, forecasts and a risk model, and statistical significance. Total recorded cost Tk 1.08 crore, of which 89% went to the vehicle fleet. Use the buttons above for the TPM programme and the illustrated equipment guide.

Prepared by: Akib Fateh, Barabkunda LPG Plant (CTG). Date: 6 November 2026

Safety first: for review by a qualified engineer

These are things that are not recorded in SAP; the work may have been done without reaching SAP. Decision support, not control.

S1 · Gas detectors54.5 months

The only SAP order for gas-monitor service is 4004850, 21 April 2022, zero cost, never closed. There is no calibration or service order after it.

Manufacturer's calibration interval; NFPA 58; LPG Rules 2004
S2 · Fire extinguishers31.0-month gap

Refill orders: 25 Aug 2022, 15 May 2023, 14 Dec 2025, 15 Jun 2026. From 15 May 2023 to 14 Dec 2025 SAP shows no refill or maintenance.

NFPA 10 (annual maintenance); Fire Prevention and Extinguishing Act 2003
S3 · Plant licences15 kinds

Last fire-licence order 11 September 2022, plant explosives licence 1 April 2023; last order for any plant licence 10 November 2023. Renewals may be recorded elsewhere; check the expiry dates.

Explosives Act 1884 and LPG Rules 2004 (Department of Explosives); Fire Service licence
S4 · Vehicle explosives licencesNone after 2023

For most LPG-carrying vehicles the last order named "Explosive" is from 2023; only CM-DHA-11-0139 has one in 2026 (Tk 80,877). SAP does not show whether the general 2026 "DOC RENEWAL" orders include this licence.

Department of Explosives vehicle licence; LPG Rules 2004
S5 · Air compressors0 of 15 released

In 2022–2026, the 15 preventive plan orders for the two compressors were only created and left idle. The only order with a cost is 4010792: an outside repair of compressor 2, Tk 2.6 lakh (30 March 2026). The filling and sealing machines run on compressed air.

Manufacturer's maintenance schedule; periodic inspection of pressure vessels
S6 · Fire-fighting system2 orders

Repair of the fire monitor's 4" gate valve (May 2023, zero cost, still open) and the fire-fighting pipeline valve (September 2025, Tk 19,300). There is no routine test order for pumps, hydrants or drenchers.

NFPA 25 (inspection and testing of water-based fire protection); NFPA 58
Executive summary

Five points

  • Safety first: the only SAP order for gas-detector service is dated 21 April 2022 (54.5 months ago); fire-extinguisher refills once had a gap of 31.0 months; renewal orders for 15 kinds of plant licence stop after 10 November 2023. Verification by a qualified engineer is required.
  • Cost: Tk 76.1 lakh on 30 identified vehicles in Jun 2025 – Jun 2026; just 17 vehicles take 80% of the cost. Highest: CM-DHA-61-0225 at Tk 9.7 lakh.
  • Process: not one of the 552 orders is technically closed (TECO); 225 (41%) were written after the work. From July 2026 to today the fleet has only 5 orders, and none in the 23 days since 14 October 2026; an estimated Tk 24.2 lakh (13.2 lakh–35.3 lakh) of cost is not yet in SAP.
  • Preventive: only 43% of fleet jobs include a scheduled service; none of the 15 compressor plan orders was ever released. The same part was repaired again within 90 days 44 times, costing Tk 8.1 lakh.
  • Forecast: a neural-network model ranks which vehicles will need a major repair (≥ Tk 50,000) in the next 3 months with AUC 0.76 (90% range 0.66–0.85), better than the past rate alone (0.63). Highest risk: 0228, 0247, 0246, 0284.

Before the analysis

Data quality: what was found and what was done

Every issue was counted. Without knowing them, the figures below would be misread.

No order has been closed

Of 552 orders, 0 are TECO/CLSD; only 5 are confirmed (CNF), and only 5 have actual start and finish dates.

What was done: Downtime and time to repair (MTTR) cannot be measured; intervals are measured from order dates.

Cost is materials only

381 orders carry a cost, and every one has a goods issue (GMPS); there is no cost without materials.

What was done: Labour and outside-service costs are not visible; cost may be understated.

A 9-month gap

Only 2 general maintenance orders in Jul 2024 – May 2025; 48 of the 67 orders of 2022–23 have zero cost.

What was done: Trends and models use the continuous data of Jun 2025 – Jun 2026.

23 silent days since the last order

The record runs to 6 November 2026, but the last order is dated 14 October 2026. At the 2026 average rate (22.2 a month) about 17 orders would be expected in these 23 days. 2026 already had a 39-day gap that was later filled by back-dated orders (median delay of such orders 63 days). So the work has most likely been done but is not yet in SAP. Since July there are 12 orders in all, 5 of them for the fleet; the first half of 2026 averaged 26.5 a month.

What was done: Missing orders are not taken to mean no work: this period is left out of forecast training and the unbooked cost is estimated separately.

Orders written after the work

225 orders are dated more than 30 days before the previous order number; median delay 25 days.

What was done: Orders are opened to book cost afterwards, not to plan work; the order date is taken as the job date.

60 ways of writing vehicle numbers

35 vehicle numbers are written 60 different ways in the descriptions (e.g. CM DA-61-0225, 61-0226, C.M.DHA 11-0137); 53 spellings of 12 common words.

What was done: Each vehicle is brought to one name using the last four digits and the equipment number.

Orders on the wrong vehicle

In 3 orders the vehicle in the description differs from the vehicle of the equipment number (e.g. 4010249); 1 has a number typo (CM-Sha-11-0247).

What was done: The vehicle in the description is used for the job count; these orders are flagged in the list.

Possible duplicate orders

4 zero-cost twin orders in 6 pairs. CM-DHA-61-0287 got tyres twice in 24 days (Tk 61,600 each time).

What was done: Zero-cost twins are left out of the job count; the rest are flagged for audit.

Other

34 have no equipment; 107 descriptions are cut at 40 characters; 21 are only created (CRTD), never released; 1 is not maintenance (vehicle hire).

What was done: The hire order is left out of the analysis.

Three costs still to verify

The cost of 3 orders (4010371, 4010372, 4010408) should be checked against the original SAP record.

What was done: Marked "cost to verify" in the list; their effect on the total is small.

Job types

Which parts the money goes on

Every fleet order is put into one of 14 categories from the words in its description; when several parts are named, the first important one is used.

By category, Jun 2025 – Jun 2026

How much job type decides cost (regression)

How well job type, series and year explain the cost of the 339 jobs with a cost (median Tk 16,526, mean Tk 27,597) was measured with 5-fold cross-validation. Best Gradient boosting: R² 0.20. So only about a fifth of the cost is explained by the description; the rest is not written down (which parts, how many). The multipliers below show how many times the cost of a scheduled service each job type usually costs.

Groups found automatically in the text (unsupervised learning)

Groups were formed automatically from the description text (vehicle numbers removed, character-level TF-IDF) with K-Means; the silhouette score is best at k = 14 (0.26). Agreement with the rule-based categories is low (ARI 0.22), because many groups form around spelling variants (e.g. schedule/schedual/shedule). This is evidence that SAP needs catalogue codes.

Preventive vs reactive

Is work planned, or done after a breakdown?

In Jun 2025 – Jun 2026, 42.6% of fleet jobs include a scheduled service (service only 20.3%, the rest service with repair); by cost it is 39.8%. In H1 2026 the share was 47.3%, against 39.2% in the previous six months. The median gap between two scheduled services is 70 days (middle half 42–101 days), with no fixed schedule. 0 of SAP's 15 plan orders (compressors) were released.

Fleet jobs by type, per quarter
Days between two maintenance jobs: Weibull distribution

A Weibull distribution is fitted to the number of days between two consecutive maintenance days of each vehicle (275 intervals). Shape β = 1.15 (90% range 1.08–1.23), scale η = 35.8 days. β a little above 1 means the chance of the next job rises slowly with time (mild wear-out). Mean interval 34.1 days; chance of another job within 30 days 56%. KS test p = 0.08, so the distribution fits the data acceptably.

SAP preventive plan orders: not one released

Forecasts and models

What is coming

Every model shows its method, training period, accuracy and range. Where a model does not beat the baseline, that is said too.

1. Forecast of the fleet's monthly cost

The fleet's monthly cost swings widely: in Jun 2025 – Jun 2026 the monthly mean is Tk 6.1 lakh with a standard deviation of Tk 3.6 lakh (variability 60%). Seven methods forecast one month ahead for each month of January–June 2026, each time using only the earlier months. Lowest error: Average to date, RMSE Tk 3.9 lakh, 35% better than naive; but MAPE is 124% because a few months have very low cost. Forecast for each coming month: Tk 6.1 lakh, 80% range Tk 0.7 lakh to 11.4 lakh. From July 2026 to 6 November 2026 only Tk 1.2 lakh has reached SAP; if work continued at the same rate, an estimated Tk 24.2 lakh (Tk 13.2 lakh–35.3 lakh) is still to be entered.

Recorded (Jun 2025 – Jun 2026)Forecast and 80% rangeRecorded since (incomplete)

2. Which vehicles need a major repair (≥ Tk 50,000) in the next 3 months

Each vehicle-month is one row (120 test rows, 22 with a major repair). Target: any job of ≥ Tk 50,000 in the next 3 months. Each model learns only from earlier months and forecasts each month of Jan 2026 – Apr 2026. Best: Neural network (MLP, mean of 10), AUC 0.76 (90% range 0.66–0.85); the vehicle's past rate alone gives 0.63. In 2,000 bootstrap resamples the neural network beats the baseline 94% of the time. The sample is small, so this sets inspection priority; it is not a certain prediction.

Which inputs help most (permutation importance)

Risk list: July–September 2026

Risk for July–September 2026 from data up to June 2026. Mean probability 19%. Major jobs of that period have so far reached SAP for 2 vehicles, 1 of them in the top ten (the rest of the data is not in yet, so this is not a full check).

3. Will any job be needed next month?

The same set-up was tested for "will any job be needed next month" (180 rows, 106 with a job). Here no machine-learning model beat the vehicle's own past rate (AUC 0.67): small jobs mostly follow each vehicle's habit, so the simple rate is enough.

4. Unusual costs (anomaly detection)

Distance of each cost from the median of the same job type (robust z, using the median and MAD) plus an Isolation Forest together flag 17 orders. They are not errors, only worth checking.

Appendix

Assumptions and limitations

Period

Trends, vehicle comparisons and models use Jun 2025 – Jun 2026, because there is a 9-month gap before it and the data after it is incomplete. Total cost includes all years.

Vehicles and job types

Vehicle numbers are brought to one name using the last four digits and the equipment number. Job types come from the description words, in 14 categories; scheduled service = any spelling of schedule, or only oil, filter and grease.

Assumptions

The order's basic start date is taken as the job date. Renewals are assumed valid for one year. Cost in taka, SAP "Total actual costs". The three-year TPM plant targets are proposed, not approved.

Limitations

No labour or outside-service cost; downtime and MTTR cannot be measured because orders are never closed; vehicle age, kilometres and running hours are missing and would improve the forecasts. The sample is small, so the models set inspection priority; they are not certain predictions.

Review

All safety observations and maintenance schedules are for review by a qualified engineer (NFPA 10, 25, 58; LPG Rules 2004). Decision support, not control.

Office TPM

Where SAP orders get stuck

The full life cycle of a maintenance order: created → released → materials and cost → confirmation → technically closed. Almost all of Barabkunda's 552 orders stop after cost posting, so downtime, time to repair (MTTR) and actual job dates cannot be measured.

Order life cycle

Share of back-dated orders, by quarter

Orders opened more than 30 days after the job date. Target ≤ 10%.

Autonomous maintenance and 5S

Operators and drivers: the first guardians of the equipment

The seven steps of Jishu Hozen, a defect-tag system and a 5S audit you can score right here. Audit scores stay only in this browser; print and sign them for the record.

Seven steps

  1. 1
    Initial cleaning

    Cleaning is inspection: find leaks, cracks and loose bolts under the dirt and attach defect tags.

    Exit criterion: Start with the carousel and pump house; every tag on the list.
  2. 2
    Remove sources of contamination and hard-to-reach places

    Stop oil, dust or gas from seeping out; make cleaning and inspection easy.

    Exit criterion: Every source fixed and cleaning time halved.
  3. 3
    Provisional standards for cleaning, lubrication and inspection

    What, how, how often, who: a one-page CLIT standard.

    Exit criterion: A CLIT card hung on every piece of equipment.
  4. 4
    General inspection

    Teach operators the parts and functions of the equipment (bolts, oil, air, electricity, pressure), then inspect.

    Exit criterion: A one-point lesson and test for each topic.
  5. 5
    Autonomous inspection

    Operators run their own checklists; duties split against the maintenance team's checklist.

    Exit criterion: Checklist compliance ≥ 95%.
  6. 6
    Standardisation

    Workplace management: fixed places for parts, tools and information; visual controls (colours, markings).

    Exit criterion: ≥ 80% in the 5S audit.
  7. 7
    Autonomous management

    Operator teams set their own targets, measure losses and run small kaizens.

    Exit criterion: Monthly team kaizen.

Defect tags (F-tags)

Blue tag

Operator can fix it (cleaning, loose bolt, label)

Red tag

Maintenance team needed (leak, crack, vibration, broken gauge)

Yellow tag

Safety risk: report immediately (gas smell, unusable extinguisher)

Every tag goes in the logbook and as an SAP notification; weekly open/closed counts on the TPM board.

LPG distribution equipment · Barabkunda

From tanker to cylinder: every piece of equipment, illustrated

21 pieces of equipment, from the storage spheres, non-return valves and butterfly valves to safety valves, pumps, filling heads, gas detectors and fire protection: what each does, what is inside, how it fails, and who maintains what, how often.

Prepared by: Akib Fateh · Barabkunda LPG Plant (CTG) · All drawings are explanatory, not to scale. Maintenance schedules are for review by a qualified engineer; manufacturer's instructions and licence conditions take precedence.

Flow diagram

Where each piece of equipment sits

From tanker unloading to storage, pumps, carousel, check-scale and dispatch, with the fire-water network below. Click any symbol to go to that equipment's full description.

Equipment guide

21 pieces of equipment

Non-return valve (swing check)

Non-return valve (NRV), swing check
Valves and pipelines
What it does
Lets flow pass in one direction only and closes by itself as soon as reverse flow starts. Stops liquid LPG or fire water from running back when a pump or compressor stops.
Where in the plant
Tanker unloading line, fire-pump discharge, pump bypass line.
How it works
A disc hung on a hinge swings up under the pressure of the flow; when flow stops or reverses, its weight and the back-pressure seat it and close the passage.

Parts

  1. 1
    BodyThe main pressure-containing shell; for LPG, carbon steel (e.g. ASTM A216 WCB) or forged steel.
  2. 2
    Cover/bonnetAccess cover; remove it to inspect the disc and seat.
  3. 3
    GasketSeal between body and cover; spiral-wound or graphite for LPG.
  4. 4
    Hinge pinThe axis the disc turns on; when worn, the disc does not seat properly.
  5. 5
    Hinge armHolds the disc from the pin.
  6. 6
    DiscThe main part that closes or opens the flow.
  7. 7
    Seat ringWhere the disc seats and seals; scratches cause leaks.
  8. 8
    Studs and nutsHold the cover; tighten to the specified torque.
  9. 9
    FlangeConnection to the pipe; rating equal to or above the line pressure.
Special requirements for LPG
  • Flow direction is marked with an arrow on the body; installed backwards, the line stays shut.
  • In horizontal lines install with the cover on top; in vertical lines only for upward flow.
  • Too close behind a pump, turbulence makes the disc flutter (chattering).
Common failures and symptoms
FailureWhat you see
Worn disc or seatReverse flow after the pump stops; the pump spins backwards
Seized hinge pinValve does not open, low flow, high pressure drop
Disc chatteringKnocking noise, vibration, fast pin wear
Water/liquid hammerBanging in the pipe on sudden closure, loose supports
Maintenance (CLIT) and KPIs
TaskHow oftenWhoType
External leak check (soap water/detector) and listen for noiseDailyOperatorI
Check the cover studs are tightMonthlyTechnicianT
Stop the pump and check for reverse flowQuarterlyTechnicianI
Open up and inspect disc, seat and pin; replace the gasketYearly or at shutdownEngineerI

KPI to track: Reverse rotation after pump stop (yes/no), pressure drop ΔP, leak incidents

Non-return valve (dual-plate wafer)

Non-return valve (NRV), dual-plate wafer check
Valves and pipelines
What it does
Works like a swing check but is lighter and smaller; two half-plates close fast under spring force, so there is less hammer.
Where in the plant
LPG filling-pump discharge, lines with little space, fire-water ring main.
How it works
A wafer body sits between two flanges. Two semicircular plates on a central pin open like the pages of a book; as soon as flow starts to fall, torsion springs close them before reverse flow begins.

Parts

  1. 1
    Wafer bodyClamped between two flanges by studs.
  2. 2
    Plates (two)Semicircular; turn on the pin.
  3. 3
    Hinge pinThe plates' axis.
  4. 4
    Torsion springCloses the plates quickly; when worn, closing is late.
  5. 5
    Stop pinLimits how far the plates open.
  6. 6
    SeatMetal or elastomer seat in the body.
  7. 7
    Stud bolts and flangesClamp the wafer; tighten evenly.
Special requirements for LPG
  • An elastomer seat must be an LPG-compatible material (e.g. NBR/FKM).
  • Keep straight pipe before and after, or the plates flutter.
Common failures and symptoms
FailureWhat you see
Broken or weak springLate closing, hammer
Plates rubbing the pipe's inner wallPlates do not open fully, pressure drop
Seat wearSeepage in the reverse direction
Maintenance (CLIT) and KPIs
TaskHow oftenWhoType
Listen for vibration and noiseDailyOperatorI
Flange leaks and studsMonthlyTechnicianT
Reverse-flow testQuarterlyTechnicianI
Open up and inspect plates, pin and springsYearlyEngineerI

KPI to track: Hammer events on pump trips, pressure drop

Butterfly valve

Butterfly valve
Valves and pipelines
What it does
A round disc turns 90° around the stem to open or close the line. A light, low-cost isolation valve for large-diameter lines.
Where in the plant
Fire-water mains and pump headers, cooling-water and air lines; on LPG only the high-performance fire-safe type (triple-offset).
How it works
Turning the handle or gearbox turns the disc through the stem; the line is closed when the disc edge presses into the liner. A part-open position throttles flow, but holding it there for long wears the seat.

Parts

  1. 1
    Body (lug/wafer)The lug type holds pressure on one side even with the other side's pipe removed.
  2. 2
    Seat linerEPDM/NBR or PTFE; seals against the disc.
  3. 3
    DiscStainless steel or ductile iron.
  4. 4
    Stem/shaftCarries the handle's rotation to the disc.
  5. 5
    BushingKeeps the stem straight and reduces friction.
  6. 6
    Neck and O-ring/glandStops leaks out along the stem.
  7. 7
    Top flange (ISO 5211)Mounting pattern for a gearbox or actuator.
  8. 8
    Gearbox and handwheelTurns a large valve slowly, preventing sudden closure (hammer).
  9. 9
    Position indicatorShows open or closed from a distance.
Special requirements for LPG
  • Fire-water isolation valves must always be locked or sealed open and clearly marked.
  • An ordinary rubber-seated butterfly valve does not belong on a liquid-LPG line; use a fire-safe ball valve or a high-performance butterfly there.
Common failures and symptoms
FailureWhat you see
Liner swollen or tornDoes not close fully, hard to turn
Rusted gearboxHandwheel seizes; cannot be opened in an emergency
Stem-seal leakWater/gas at the neck
Maintenance (CLIT) and KPIs
TaskHow oftenWhoType
Check the open-position seal and lock are in placeWeeklyOperatorI
Stroke fully open and closed (exercise)QuarterlyTechnicianI
Grease the gearbox, lubricate the stemHalf-yearlyTechnicianL
Inspect liner and discYearly or at shutdownEngineerI

KPI to track: Valves found stuck when exercised, valves open without a seal

Ball valve (fire-safe)

Ball valve, fire-safe, cavity-relieved
Valves and pipelines
What it does
A ball with a bore turns 90° to open or close the line instantly. The main isolation valve on LPG lines.
Where in the plant
Tanker unloading, sphere inlet and outlet, pump suction and discharge, filling header.
How it works
Turning the lever turns the ball; with the bore in line with the pipe it is fully open, crosswise it is closed. PTFE seats press against the ball to seal.

Parts

  1. 1
    Body (3-piece)The centre section comes out to change the seats.
  2. 2
    End capsFlanged or welded connection to the pipe.
  3. 3
    BallStainless steel, chrome-plated.
  4. 4
    Seats (PTFE)Primary seal.
  5. 5
    Fire-safe graphite sealIf the PTFE melts in a fire, the metal/graphite seal keeps the leak limited (tested to API 607/ISO 10497).
  6. 6
    Stem (blow-out proof)Cannot be blown out by pressure.
  7. 7
    Gland packingStops leaks along the stem; can be tightened when needed.
  8. 8
    Lever and lockShows position; can be locked out.
  9. 9
    Cavity relief holeWhen liquid LPG trapped inside the closed ball expands with heat, it vents the pressure upstream; this is why the valve has a flow direction.
  10. 10
    Anti-static springKeeps electrical contact between ball, stem and body to prevent sparks.
Special requirements for LPG
  • Liquid LPG trapped between two closed valves builds dangerous pressure as it warms: a hydrostatic relief valve is needed between them.
  • A cavity-relieved valve installed backwards relieves downstream.
Common failures and symptoms
FailureWhat you see
Seat wearSeepage when closed (passing)
Gland leakFrost or smell around the stem
Stiff stem/leverNeeds more force to turn, stays half open
Maintenance (CLIT) and KPIs
TaskHow oftenWhoType
Leak check on stem and flangesDailyOperatorI
Lever, lock and position markingWeeklyOperatorI
Tighten the gland, lubricate the stemQuarterlyTechnicianL/T
Passing test (compare pressure on both sides)Half-yearlyTechnicianI
Replace seats and sealsPer manufacturer's instructionsEngineerC

KPI to track: Number of passing valves, gland-leak incidents

Globe valve

Globe valve
Valves and pipelines
What it does
Controls flow slowly and finely, and also shuts off well. Used for pump bypass/recirculation and throttling.
Where in the plant
Filling-pump bypass line, drains and vents, instrument-air lines.
How it works
Turning the handwheel raises or lowers the disc on a threaded stem; flow enters below along an S-shaped path, passes the seat and leaves above.

Parts

  1. 1
    BodyWith an S-shaped path.
  2. 2
    BonnetHolds the stem and gland.
  3. 3
    HandwheelHandle for opening and closing.
  4. 4
    Stem (threaded)Turns rotation into up-and-down movement.
  5. 5
    Yoke and nutHolds the stem thread.
  6. 6
    Gland packingStem seal.
  7. 7
    Disc/plugControls the flow.
  8. 8
    Seat ringWhere the disc seals.
  9. 9
    PartitionForms the S-shaped path.
Special requirements for LPG
  • High pressure drop, so not used on main lines.
  • Install following the flow direction (under the disc).
Common failures and symptoms
FailureWhat you see
Disc-seat erosion (wire-drawing)Flow even when closed
Worn stem threadHandwheel spins freely
Gland leakLeak at the stem
Maintenance (CLIT) and KPIs
TaskHow oftenWhoType
Leak and position checkDailyOperatorI
Grease the stem threadQuarterlyTechnicianL
Tighten the glandQuarterlyTechnicianT
Lap or replace disc and seatYearlyEngineerC

KPI to track: Passing and gland leaks

Gate valve

Gate valve
Valves and pipelines
What it does
A wedge-shaped gate moves up and down to fully open or close the passage; fully open, the pressure drop is almost zero.
Where in the plant
Fire-water lines, fire monitors and hydrant isolation (SAP has an order for the fire monitor's 4" gate valve).
How it works
Turning the handwheel raises or lowers the gate on the stem. It is only for fully open or fully closed; held part-open, the gate vibrates and wears.

Parts

  1. 1
    BodyStraight-through path.
  2. 2
    BonnetCover for the gate and stem.
  3. 3
    HandwheelOpens and closes.
  4. 4
    Stem (rising)The rising stem shows the position.
  5. 5
    Gate (wedge)Closes the passage.
  6. 6
    SeatWhere the gate seats.
  7. 7
    Gland packingStem seal.
  8. 8
    YokeHolds the stem nut.
Special requirements for LPG
  • Closes slowly, so in an emergency shutdown rely on a ball valve or ESD valve.
  • Fire-water gate valves must be sealed open and turned regularly.
Common failures and symptoms
FailureWhat you see
Stem seized (rust)Cannot be opened in an emergency
Gate does not seat (dirt)Does not close fully
Gland leakWater seepage

TaskHow oftenWhoType
Open-position sealWeeklyOperatorI
Full open-close exerciseQuarterlyTechnicianI
Grease the stemQuarterlyTechnicianL

LPG storage sphere (spherical tank)

LPG storage sphere (Horton sphere)
StorageSafety-critical
What it does
Stores liquid LPG under pressure. A sphere spreads the pressure evenly over the whole shell, so more gas can be held for the same wall thickness. The plant's largest source of risk and its most important asset.
Where in the plant
Four spheres side by side in Barabkunda's storage area: white shell, red equator band, standing on legs, with a top platform and safety valves.
How it works
Liquid LPG from ship or tanker enters through the bottom pipe; vapour fills the upper part. Internal pressure rises and falls with temperature. Pumps draw liquid from the bottom outlet to the filling shed; the safety valves on top release excess pressure.

Parts

  1. 1
    ShellThe pressure vessel; welded steel plates. White paint absorbs less solar heat, so pressure stays lower.
  2. 2
    Liquid LPG and vapour spaceLiquid expands with heat, so the vessel must never be filled above its set maximum fill limit.
  3. 3
    Legs and bracingCarry the weight of the shell and liquid to the ground; cross bracing takes wind and earthquake loads.
  4. 4
    Fireproofing on the legsIn a fire, bare steel legs weaken quickly and the sphere can collapse; concrete or fireproof coating buys time.
  5. 5
    Twin safety valvesTwo PSVs with a changeover valve: the sphere stays protected while one is taken out for testing.
  6. 6
    Level gauge and high-level switchMeasures liquid height; an independent high-high level switch stops filling.
  7. 7
    Pressure and temperature gaugesRecorded daily; a sudden pressure rise is the first sign of danger.
  8. 8
    Water-spray ringKeeps the whole shell cool with water in a fire or excess heat (deluge).
  9. 9
    Bottom outlet, internal valve and ESDThe most hazardous point: a flange leak here releases liquid; the remotely closed valve sits here.
  10. 10
    Stairs and top platformAccess to the PSVs and level gauge; needs handrails and lighting.
  11. 11
    EarthingDischarges lightning and static electricity; the resistance must be measured regularly.
Special requirements for LPG
  • The maximum fill limit is set in the design and the licence (usually about 85% of volume); both the high-level alarm and the independent high-high switch must be kept working.
  • When a sphere heats up in a fire, the pressure rises and the PSV opens; even so, an overheated shell can weaken and rupture (BLEVE). That is why the water spray, fireproofed legs and remotely operated bottom valve are all life-saving.
  • Periodic inspection and testing of the pressure vessel per the Department of Explosives licence conditions and the LPG Rules 2004; NFPA 58.
  • SAP has no maintenance order under the name sphere, PSV, level gauge or water spray: either it is recorded under another name, or not recorded at all.
Common failures and symptoms
FailureWhat you see
Leak at the bottom flange or valveFrost, smell, detector alarm
Corrosion under the coatingCracks in the fireproofing, rust stains; weakened legs
Level gauge reading wrongRisk of overfilling; gauge and high-level switch disagree
Foundation settlementUneven leg heights, bent bracing
Blocked spray nozzlesParts of the shell stay dry in the test
Maintenance (CLIT) and KPIs
TaskHow oftenWhoType
Record level, pressure and temperature; check the maximum fill limitDailyOperatorI
Walk around: leaks, frost, bottom valves, stairsDailyOperatorI
Test the high-level alarm and high-high switchQuarterlyEngineerI
Full-flow water-spray test and nozzle cleaningYearlyEngineerC/I
Inspect leg fireproofing, foundations and paintYearlyEngineerI
Measure earthing resistanceYearlyEngineerI
Periodic inspection and testing of the pressure vesselAs per licence conditionsApproved outside contractorI

KPI to track: Maximum-fill violations (target zero), high-level switch test compliance, dry areas in the water-spray test

Pressure safety (relief) valve

Pressure safety valve (PSV / PRV)
StorageSafety-critical
What it does
Opens by itself and releases gas when tank or line pressure exceeds the set limit, so the vessel does not burst. The last line of defence.
Where in the plant
On top of each storage sphere (in pairs with a changeover valve), pump discharge, tankers, and the line between two closed valves (hydrostatic relief).
How it works
A spring holds the disc down on the nozzle. When the pressure below exceeds the spring force, the disc lifts; when pressure falls, it reseats.

Parts

  1. 1
    Inlet nozzleConnection to the vessel; any isolation valve here must be locked open.
  2. 2
    DiscKeeps the nozzle closed.
  3. 3
    SeatWhere the disc seats.
  4. 4
    GuideKeeps the disc moving straight up and down.
  5. 5
    SpindleCarries the spring force to the disc.
  6. 6
    SpringSets the set pressure.
  7. 7
    Spring washersHold the spring.
  8. 8
    Adjusting screw and lock nutSets the set pressure; sealed after testing.
  9. 9
    Cap and sealPrevent unauthorised changes.
  10. 10
    OutletReleases gas at a safe height through a tall vent pipe with a rain cap.
Special requirements for LPG
  • Set pressure follows the vessel's design pressure and the licence conditions; it must never be changed locally.
  • Testing and resetting only on an approved bench, tagged with the date and set pressure.
  • With two PSVs and a changeover valve, one can be removed for testing without leaving the tank unprotected.
Common failures and symptoms
FailureWhat you see
Opening below set pressure or seeping (simmering)Frost or smell at the vent, gas loss
Stuck (dirt, rust, paint)Does not open even at overpressure: the most dangerous failure
Water or a bird's nest in the vent pipeBlocked flow
Broken sealUnknown whether the set pressure was changed
Maintenance (CLIT) and KPIs
TaskHow oftenWhoType
Check vent pipe, rain cap and sealWeeklyOperatorI
Check the inlet isolation valve is open and lockedWeeklyOperatorI
Bench pop test and reset, taggedYearly or per licence/manufacturerApproved outside contractorI
Inspect and replace nozzle, disc, springPer manufacturer's instructionsEngineerC

KPI to track: Share of PSVs tested on time (target 100%), set-pressure deviation in tests

Excess flow valve

Excess flow valve (EFV)
StorageSafety-critical
What it does
Closes by itself when flow suddenly rises because a pipe or hose has burst, stopping the tank from emptying.
Where in the plant
On the sphere's bottom liquid outlet and vapour line, and on tanker outlets (often with an internal valve).
How it works
A spring holds the poppet open. When flow exceeds the set limit, the drag of the flow pushes the poppet onto the seat. Once pressure on both sides equalises through a small bleed hole, it reopens.

Parts

  1. 1
    BodyThreaded or flanged into the line.
  2. 2
    PoppetThe closing part.
  3. 3
    SpringSets the closing flow limit.
  4. 4
    SeatWhere the poppet seats.
  5. 5
    Bleed holeSlowly equalises pressure after closing.
  6. 6
    Stop/retainerLimits the poppet when open.
Special requirements for LPG
  • The rated flow must be above the line's normal flow but below the flow of a full rupture.
  • It does not close on a partial leak or small hole; then ESD and gas detectors are what you rely on.
Common failures and symptoms
FailureWhat you see
Poppet stuck openDoes not close on a rupture
Repeated nuisance closingFlow cut off at pump start (wrong rating)
Maintenance (CLIT) and KPIs
TaskHow oftenWhoType
Watch for nuisance closing at start-upDailyOperatorI
Function test (at controlled flow)Yearly or at shutdownEngineerI

KPI to track: Share of EFVs passing the test

Emergency shutdown valve

Emergency shutdown / remote-operated valve (ESDV/ROV)
Receipt and transferSafety-critical
What it does
Closes the line within seconds, remotely or automatically, in an emergency. Closes even if air or power is lost (fail-closed).
Where in the plant
Tanker unloading point, sphere bottom liquid outlet, start of the filling header.
How it works
Instrument air in a pneumatic cylinder compresses a spring and holds the valve open. When an ESD button is pressed, a gas detector alarms or a fusible plug melts in a fire, the air vents and the spring closes the valve.

Parts

  1. 1
    Ball valve bodyFire-safe ball valve.
  2. 2
    Actuator (scotch-yoke)Turns straight-line motion into a 90° rotation.
  3. 3
    Return springCloses the valve when air is lost.
  4. 4
    Pneumatic cylinderHolds the valve open with air pressure.
  5. 5
    Solenoid valveVents the air on an ESD signal.
  6. 6
    Limit switch boxReports open/closed to the control room.
  7. 7
    Air supply/filter regulatorSupplies clean, dry air.
  8. 8
    ESD button and fusible plugClosing signal by hand or by fire heat.
Special requirements for LPG
  • The closing time (stroke time) must stay within its limit and be measured in tests.
  • Water in the instrument air can freeze the solenoid in cold weather: air-compressor and dryer maintenance is directly a safety matter.
Common failures and symptoms
FailureWhat you see
Weak actuator springPartial closing
Solenoid stuckDoes not close even on signal
Faulty limit switchWrong status in the control room
Leak in the air lineValve closes by itself and production stops
Maintenance (CLIT) and KPIs
TaskHow oftenWhoType
Check status lamps and air pressureDailyOperatorI
Partial-stroke testMonthlyTechnicianI
Full closing test with stroke time recordedQuarterlyEngineerI
Inspect solenoid, filter regulator, fusible plugsHalf-yearlyTechnicianC/I
ESD loop test (from button to valve)YearlyEngineerI

KPI to track: ESD test success rate (target 100%), stroke time

Y-strainer

Y-strainer
Receipt and transfer
What it does
Catches weld spatter, rust and dirt in the flow so pumps, valves and filling heads are not damaged.
Where in the plant
Suction of every LPG pump and compressor, tanker unloading line, upstream of flow meters.
How it works
Flow passes through the screen in the Y-shaped branch; dirt stays in the screen. As the screen fills, the pressure difference across it (ΔP) rises.

Parts

  1. 1
    BodyY-shaped.
  2. 2
    ScreenStainless mesh.
  3. 3
    Cap and gasketRemove to take out the screen.
  4. 4
    Blow-off valveSmall valve for flushing out dirt.
  5. 5
    Inlet/outlet pressure gaugesMeasure ΔP.
Special requirements for LPG
  • Isolate, depressurise and gas-free the line before opening the cap (permit-to-work).
  • A full screen lowers pump suction pressure and causes cavitation.
Common failures and symptoms
FailureWhat you see
Screen fullHigh ΔP, low pump flow, noise
Torn screenAbnormally low ΔP, dirt in the pump
Cap gasket leakSmell or frost
Maintenance (CLIT) and KPIs
TaskHow oftenWhoType
Read ΔP and write it in the logbookDailyOperatorI
Clean the screenWhen ΔP exceeds the limit, or monthlyTechnicianC
Replace screen and gasketYearlyTechnicianC

KPI to track: ΔP trend; cleaning interval

Pressure gauge (Bourdon tube)

Pressure gauge, Bourdon tube
Storage
What it does
Shows tank, pump and line pressure directly. The operator's first warning signal.
Where in the plant
Each sphere, pump and compressor suction and discharge, both sides of strainers, filling header.
How it works
As pressure rises, the curved Bourdon tube tries to straighten; its movement turns the pointer through a link, sector gear and pinion.

Parts

  1. 1
    Dial and scaleFull scale is best at about twice the normal working pressure.
  2. 2
    PointerShows the pressure.
  3. 3
    Bourdon tubeChanges its curve with pressure.
  4. 4
    LinkTakes up the tube's movement.
  5. 5
    Sector gear and pinionMagnify the movement.
  6. 6
    HairspringRemoves backlash.
  7. 7
    Socket (thread)Connection to the line.
  8. 8
    Glycerine fill and blow-out plugSteadies the pointer under vibration; vents pressure outward if the tube bursts.
  9. 9
    Isolation valveLets the gauge be removed for calibration.
Special requirements for LPG
  • Stainless Bourdon tube and socket for LPG.
  • A red mark at the maximum allowed pressure lets the operator see it at a glance.
Common failures and symptoms
FailureWhat you see
Does not return to zeroCalibration has drifted
Pointer fluttersVibration or low glycerine
Broken or fogged glassCannot be read
Maintenance (CLIT) and KPIs
TaskHow oftenWhoType

LPG pump (sliding-vane)

LPG transfer pump, sliding vane
Filling and checking
What it does
Sends liquid LPG from the spheres to the filling carousel or to tankers. The fire-water network has separate fire pumps.
Where in the plant
Pump house: spheres to filling header; fire pump house.
How it works
Vanes sit in slots of an off-centre rotor; as it turns, the vanes move out and touch the liner. The space between vanes is large at suction and small at discharge, pushing the liquid out.

Parts

  1. 1
    CasingHolds the pressure.
  2. 2
    Cam/linerRubbing surface for the vanes; replaceable.
  3. 3
    RotorCarries the vanes.
  4. 4
    VanesWearing parts.
  5. 5
    ShaftTakes the motor's rotation.
  6. 6
    Mechanical sealStops LPG leaking along the shaft; the most important inspection point.
  7. 7
    Internal relief valveReturns pressure to suction when the discharge is shut.
  8. 8
    SuctionNeeds a strainer and vapour-free liquid.
  9. 9
    DischargeWith NRV and bypass.
Special requirements for LPG
  • Liquid LPG is close to its boiling point, so any drop in suction pressure makes vapour (cavitation): keep the suction line short and straight and the strainer clean.
  • Motor and junction box must be flameproof (Ex d); earthing and bonding intact.
  • Running dry ruins the vanes and seal.
Common failures and symptoms
FailureWhat you see
Mechanical-seal leakFrost on the shaft, smell, detector alarm
Vane wearLow pressure and flow, slow filling
CavitationCrackling noise, vibration
Bearing wearRising temperature and vibration
Maintenance (CLIT) and KPIs
TaskHow oftenWhoType
Check seal leaks, noise, temperature and vibrationDailyOperatorI
Record suction and discharge pressureDailyOperatorI
Grease bearings; check coupling and boltsMonthlyTechnicianL/T
Vibration analysis and motor insulation testQuarterlyTechnicianI
Replace vanes, liner, sealBy running hours (manufacturer)EngineerC

KPI to track: MTBF (hours), seal-leak incidents, discharge-pressure trend

LPG compressor

LPG vapour compressor (reciprocating)
Receipt and transfer
What it does
To unload a tanker it draws vapour from storage and pressurises the tanker, which pushes liquid LPG through the pipe into storage; at the end it also recovers the vapour.
Where in the plant
Compressor house next to the unloading bay.
How it works
A crankshaft-driven piston compresses vapour in the cylinder. Turning the 4-way valve reverses the direction. A liquid trap stops liquid entering the cylinder.

Parts

  1. 1
    CylinderCompression chamber.
  2. 2
    Piston and ringsWearing parts.
  3. 3
    Suction/discharge valvesPlate valves; a broken one cuts capacity.
  4. 4
    Piston-rod packingStops gas reaching the crankcase.
  5. 5
    CrossheadGuides the rod in a straight line.
  6. 6
    Connecting rodMotion from the crank.
  7. 7
    CrankshaftThe motor's rotation.
  8. 8
    Liquid trapSeparates liquid; stops the compressor at high level.
  9. 9
    4-way valveSwitches between unloading and vapour recovery.
Special requirements for LPG
  • Liquid entering the cylinder causes instant major damage: test the liquid trap's level switch regularly.
  • During unloading the tanker's earthing, wheel chocks and breakaway must be connected.
Common failures and symptoms
FailureWhat you see
Broken valve plateLow capacity, high discharge temperature
Packing leakGas at the crankcase vent
Level switch not workingLiquid gets in and breaks the piston/rod
Maintenance (CLIT) and KPIs
TaskHow oftenWhoType
Oil level, pressure, temperature, noiseDailyOperatorL/I
Drain the liquid trap and test the level switchWeeklyTechnicianI
Belts/coupling, filtersMonthlyTechnicianC/T
Inspect valve plates and packingBy running hoursEngineerI
Change oil and filtersAs per manufacturerTechnicianL

KPI to track: Unloading time (minutes/tonne), discharge temperature

Loading hose and breakaway coupling

Loading hose with breakaway coupling
Receipt and transferSafety-critical
What it does
The plant's connection to the tanker. If the vehicle moves off by mistake, the coupling separates instead of the hose tearing, and both sides close.
Where in the plant
Liquid and vapour hoses at the unloading bay.
How it works
A break bolt or ring fails at a set pull; spring poppets in both halves close at once, so only a little gas escapes.

Parts

  1. 1
    HoseLPG-rated stainless braided or rubber; test date marked.
  2. 2
    Breakaway couplingSeparates safely.
  3. 3
    Self-closing poppetsClose both sides.
  4. 4
    Break bolt/ringBreaks at a set pull; a new set is needed after it breaks.
  5. 5
    CouplerConnection to the tanker.
  6. 6
    Earthing clampDischarges static electricity; attach before connecting.
Special requirements for LPG
  • Hose hydrostatic tests and expiry dates must be recorded; out-of-date hoses must not be used.
  • Before unloading: wheel chocks, engine off, earthing, ESD button within reach.
Common failures and symptoms
FailureWhat you see
Cracked, swollen hose or torn braidLeak, risk of the hose bursting
Worn coupler sealLeak at the connection
Broken earthing cableRisk of sparks
Maintenance (CLIT) and KPIs
TaskHow oftenWhoType
Visual check and earthing before every useEvery unloadingOperatorI
Inspect seals and couplerMonthlyTechnicianI
Hose pressure testYearly or per manufacturerApproved outside contractorI

KPI to track: Out-of-date hoses (target zero)

Filling head and weighing platform

Carousel filling head and weighing platform
Filling and checking
What it does
Fills each cylinder on the carousel with a set weight of LPG. Every error in the weight-accuracy report starts here.
Where in the plant
The carousel in the filling shed (each head has its own number).
How it works
When a cylinder sits on the platform, the head presses onto the cylinder valve and opens it. The load cell measures weight; at the set weight (net 12 kg + tare) the controller closes the filling valve.

Parts

  1. 1
    Filling headConnects to the cylinder valve.
  2. 2
    Pneumatic actuatorPresses the head down and lifts it.
  3. 3
    Filling valve and sealOpens and closes the flow; a worn seal means leaks and wrong weight.
  4. 4
    LPG hose and swivelSupply to the rotating carousel.
  5. 5
    Weighing platformWhere the cylinder sits.
  6. 6
    Load cellMeasures weight; if its calibration drifts, every cylinder gets too much or too little gas.
  7. 7
    Controller and displaySet weight and cut-off.
  8. 8
    Cylinder valveWhat the head seats on.
Special requirements for LPG
  • Because of valve-closing delay and gas left in the pipe, a little more than the set weight goes in (in-flight): it needs regular compensation.
  • Each head has its own calibration; the weight-accuracy report flags heads 5, 13, 21, 6, 11 and 14.
Common failures and symptoms
FailureWhat you see
Load-cell zero driftOne head consistently high or low
Worn filling-valve sealLeak, late cut-off
Dirt or rubbing on the platformWrong weight
Low air pressureHead does not seat properly
Maintenance (CLIT) and KPIs
TaskHow oftenWhoType
Zero point and leaks of every headEvery shiftOperatorI
Check every head on a test weightDailyOperatorI
Inspect seals and hosesWeeklyTechnicianI
Load-cell calibration (on certified weights)Monthly, or when the calibration report shows a deviationTechnicianI
Replace filling valve and sealsAs per manufacturerTechnicianC

KPI to track: Weight accuracy: mean error, % within ±150 g, Cpk

Cylinder valve (self-closing)

Cylinder valve, self-closing
Filling and checking
What it does
The valve on the neck of a 12 kg domestic cylinder. It closes by itself as soon as the regulator is removed.
Where in the plant
On every cylinder; inspected before filling and leak-tested after.
How it works
Fitting the regulator pushes the poppet down and opens the passage; removing it lets the spring press the poppet onto the O-ring and close it.

Parts

  1. 1
    Brass bodyCorrosion-resistant.
  2. 2
    Taper threadSeats tightly in the cylinder neck.
  3. 3
    PoppetOpens and closes the passage.
  4. 4
    SpringAutomatic closing.
  5. 5
    O-ringThe main seal; the part replaced most often.
  6. 6
    Regulator collarHolds the regulator.
  7. 7
    Protective capProtects against dust and knocks; also acts as a seal.
Special requirements for LPG
  • A leak test of every valve after filling (water bath or electronic) is mandatory.
  • Fill a cylinder only after checking its own retest date under the Gas Cylinder Rules 1991.
Common failures and symptoms
FailureWhat you see
Worn O-ringLeak through the valve
Poppet stuckDoes not close
Damaged threadLeak at the neck

TaskHow oftenWhoType

Leak testEvery cylinder, after fillingOperatorI

Gas detector (fixed)

Fixed gas detector
Fire and gas safetySafety-critical
What it does
Measures LPG concentration in the air and, at a set fraction of the lower explosive limit (LEL), raises an alarm and triggers ESD.
Where in the plant
Filling shed, pump and compressor house, unloading bay, sphere bottom-valve area.
How it works
A catalytic or infrared sensor detects LPG and shows %LEL. Usually a warning at 20% LEL and an alarm with shutdown at 40% LEL.

Parts

  1. 1
    Transmitter and displayShows %LEL and sends it to the control room.
  2. 2
    SensorCatalytic or IR.
  3. 3
    Sintered flame arrestorKeeps a flame inside the sensor from getting out.
  4. 4
    Splash guardProtects against water and dust.
  5. 5
    Cable glandFlameproof connection.
  6. 6
    %LEL scale and limitsWarning and alarm levels.
  7. 7
    Calibration cup and gasTest with gas of known concentration.
Special requirements for LPG
  • LPG vapour is heavier than air, so detectors must be mounted near the floor (usually within 30 cm).
  • Silicone, sulphur or too much gas can poison a catalytic sensor so it loses sensitivity: only a bump test tells you whether the sensor still works.
  • SAP's only order for gas-monitor service is from April 2022.
Common failures and symptoms
FailureWhat you see
Sensor poisoned or expiredShows zero even with gas present: the most dangerous failure
Zero driftFalse alarms
Dirt-clogged sinterSlow response
Maintenance (CLIT) and KPIs
TaskHow oftenWhoType
Check display and fault lampsDailyOperatorI
Bump test (response to gas)Monthly or per manufacturerTechnicianI
Full calibrationUsually 3–6 months (per manufacturer)TechnicianI
Replace sensorAt end of lifeTechnicianC
Full loop test from alarm to ESDYearlyEngineerI

KPI to track: Share of detectors calibrated on time (target 100%)

Deluge (water-spray) system

Deluge / water-spray system
Fire and gas safetySafety-critical
What it does
When fire or heat is detected, sprays water on the storage spheres, carousel and unloading bay to keep them cool so no vessel overheats and ruptures.
Where in the plant
The whole shell and legs of the storage spheres, the filling shed, the tanker bay.
How it works
When pressure in the detection line drops (a heat bulb breaks or a solenoid opens), the deluge valve's clapper opens and all the open nozzles spray water at once.

Parts

  1. 1
    Deluge valveClosed in normal conditions.
  2. 2
    Clapper/diaphragmOpens on a pressure difference.
  3. 3
    Trim and solenoidControls actuation.
  4. 4
    Detection lineHeat-sensitive bulbs or detectors.
  5. 5
    Isolation butterfly valveNormally open and sealed.
  6. 6
    Spray nozzlesWater does not reach where they are blocked.
  7. 7
    Alarm gongSignals water flow.
  8. 8
    Drain and test valveDrains water after a test.
Special requirements for LPG
  • Under NFPA 25: regular inspection and a yearly full-flow test; check for blocked nozzles.
  • Run the fire pumps (diesel and electric) every week.
  • SAP has no routine test order for pumps, hydrants or the deluge system.
Common failures and symptoms
FailureWhat you see
Blocked nozzles (rust, dirt)Water does not reach some areas
Clapper stuckDoes not actuate
Isolation valve left closedThe whole system out of action
